9.9 — Encryption: Keys, TLS & Public Key

When you pushed to GitHub, the URL said https — and your repo crossed the public internet unread by every router along the way. The page you are reading right now is served the same way, and the padlock in your address bar is the thing this lesson explains. Today: how a secret crosses an open network twice, why two keys are better than one, and the one math fact protecting everything you own.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I keep a message secret in transit?”
Break It Down~10 min

A message has to cross a network anybody can listen to, and arrive readable by exactly one person. "Keep it secret" is a wish; the work is the five decisions underneath it.

First, before anything else: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Choose the kind of lock: one shared key, or a pairwhat does this part do?Read: the symmetric-versus-asymmetric table in this lesson's Concept Lab, and the two matching sections of the Encryption reference page
  2. Get the right public key into the other machine's handswhat does this part do?Read: the certificate fields you read off your own site in Step 2 of the Build Lab below, and "What does a certificate prove?" on the Encryption reference page
  3. Trade one round of slow work for a whole session of fast workwhat does this part do?Read: the six-step handshake in the Concept Lab above
  4. Decide how many bits the key has to bewhat does this part do?Read: the bit-width discussion in 9.1, and the RSA paragraph on the Encryption reference page
  5. Say what the padlock protects, and what it leaves exposedwhat does this part do?Read: the packet journey in 9.8, and the Hashing section of the Encryption reference page

The split is the whole lesson, because "keep it secret" is a wish and these five are decisions. Three of them are choices you make before a single byte moves — which lock, how many bits, what the certificate has to prove — and they are the three the exam asks about. The last one is the one everybody skips: knowing what the mechanism does NOT cover is what stops you trusting a green padlock further than it can carry you.

The test: could you answer this part out loud, in one sentence, with no computer in front of you? "Use encryption" points at nothing. "Find out whose public key this is" points at a certificate you can open and read field by field.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Your own course site is served over HTTPS, and the subject of its certificate is not the address you typed. What is the browser actually matching against the host name — and does that certificate tell you anything about whether the site is honest?

TLS protects the channel, not the endpoints. Your game sends a high score to a leaderboard over HTTPS: name two things an attacker can still do even though the padlock is green.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Symmetric — one shared key. The Caesar cipher you probably did in elementary school: shift letters by a key (3: CAT → FDW). Same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, simple, and cursed by one problem: to agree on the key, you must already have a secure channel. The internet never had one, and that is the whole reason symmetric encryption could not be the answer on its own.

Asymmetric — two keys, a public pair. In the 1970s, math (huge prime numbers) delivered the miracle: you publish a PUBLIC key anyone can use to lock messages to you, and keep a PRIVATE key that is the only thing that unlocks them. Publishing the lock does not reveal the key — and that is not a slogan, it is the shape of the pair. One half can only lock and the other half can only open, so publishing the locking half costs you nothing. That is why "public key encryption" is not a contradiction. RSA-2048: the public number is 617 digits long and was built by multiplying two primes of about 309 digits each. Multiplying them takes a microsecond; pulling them back apart would take the world's computers longer than your lifetime. The exam wants the IDEA, not the factoring.

Symmetric (AES)Asymmetric (RSA)
KeysOne shared secretPublic + private pair
SpeedVery fastSlow
Perfect atBulk data — the bytes you actually sendProving identity and handing over a key — the handshake

TLS — the handshake (https). The web uses BOTH: asymmetric to establish trust, symmetric for the actual conversation. When you see the lock icon:

1. Browser → github.com:  "hello"
2. Server → browser:    certificate + its PUBLIC key
3. Browser checks the certificate against trusted authorities
4. Browser generates a random SESSION key, encrypts it with the
   server's public key, sends it
5. Server decrypts it with its private key — the ONLY one who can
6. Both switch to fast symmetric encryption with the shared key

Step 3 is what "certificate" means — a third party vouches that this public key really belongs to github.com. Without it, anyone on your wifi could impersonate the site and hand you THEIR key (a man-in-the-middle attack).

Four sentences the exam writes its wrong answers from.
  • "Public key encryption" is not a contradiction. The pair is not one secret written down twice. One half can only lock; only the other half opens. So publishing the locking half gives nothing away — and the public key cannot decrypt what it encrypted. That single fact is a whole exam question.
  • A certificate asserts exactly one thing: that the public key inside it belongs to the name inside it, according to the authority that signed it. It does not assert that the site is honest, careful, or run by the company you think it is. A green padlock says your bytes are going to the machine named in the certificate. It says nothing else, and it is not a safety rating.
  • TLS protects the channel, not the endpoints. The routers in between cannot read your push — but the server at the far end reads every byte of it, and so does anything downstream of that server. Nor is the connection invisible: somebody watching still sees which machine you contacted, when, and how much you sent.
  • A hash is not encryption. No key, no way back — a fingerprint rather than a lockbox. That is why a stolen password database is a different size of disaster from a stolen key, and why the fix is a salt rather than a longer key.

Socratic

Why does TLS not simply use asymmetric encryption for everything (hint: your 2 MB project push at RSA speed)? The exam phrasing: "explain how symmetric and asymmetric encryption are EACH used in secure transactions" — write the one-sentence version now.

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — caesar by hand. Encrypt "BOSS" with key 3 on paper (ERVV). Pass to a partner who decrypts. Then: which letter appeared twice in the ciphertext — and why does that PATTERN (frequency analysis) break Caesar without knowing the key at all? Weak ciphers die to the STATISTICS of language, not to brute force.

Step 2 — read a real certificate. You do not have to go far for one: the page you are reading now is served over HTTPS, from aramansell.github.io. Click the padlock in the address bar and open the certificate. Then read its fields and say what each one is for: the subject, the issuer, the valid dates, and the public key info. Two of them will surprise you. The subject is not the address you typed — it reads *.github.io, a single wildcard certificate covering every GitHub Pages site — and the browser accepts it because the certificate's list of names matches the host you asked for. And the lifetime is short: the day this page was last checked the certificate ran from 2 August to 31 October and was issued by Let's Encrypt, which are values you should expect to differ from yours. Read your own; do not copy mine.

Then go and look at two that are deliberately broken. self-signed.badssl.com presents a certificate signed by nobody at all, and expired.badssl.com presents one whose dates have run out. Read the browser's refusal on each and find the field it names: that field is step 3 of the handshake above, failing in front of you. Do not click through either one — a certificate warning is the browser telling you step 3 did not pass.

Step 3 — your git connection. git remote -v in your project. Is it an https or an ssh URL? Both are encrypted. SSH is the asymmetric idea with a different protocol: your ssh keypair IS your public/private pair (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub vs the private file). If you set up GitHub Desktop, it did https + TLS. Either way, your pushes have been unread to every router (9.8) since day one.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain symmetric vs asymmetric with a use case for each
  • Narrate the TLS handshake's six steps and where certificates fit
  • Read a real certificate and name what its fields prove
  • Explain why hashing is not encryption, and what a salt buys
  • Name the parts of keeping a message secret, in the order they are decided, and say where each one is written down
  • Say what a certificate proves and what it does not, and why the public key cannot undo its own lock
  • Explain why TLS protects the channel and not the endpoints
